edits.before:
Those who disbelieve, and therefore they do not truly believe.

The point is not mere verbal unbelief. The next ayah immediately shows what this disbelief looks like socially: it cannot keep covenant with taqwa.
edits.after:
Those who disbelieve, so they will not believe.

The commentaries read this as persistence, not as a comment on the quality of some hidden inner faith. Al-Muyassar glosses them as *al-kuffar al-musirrun 'ala al-kufr* - the disbelievers who insist on staying in disbelief - and al-Tabari unpacks the phrase plainly: they do not affirm the messengers of Allah and do not acknowledge His revelation. The next ayah immediately shows what this entrenched disbelief looks like socially: it cannot keep covenant with taqwa.
edits.evidence: al-Muyassar 8:55: "الكفار المصرُّون على الكفر، فهم لا يصدقون رسل الله". al-Tabari 8:55: "﴿فهم لا يؤمنون﴾ ، يقول: فهم لا يصدِّقون رسلَ الله، ولا يقرُّون بوحيه وتنزيله".

edits.before: So this is not random hostility from strangers. There was a covenant. Terms were known. A public moral bond had already been entered.
edits.after:
So this is not random hostility from strangers. There was a covenant. Terms were known. A public moral bond had already been entered.

The commentaries also tell us who this was revealed about. Al-Jalalayn opens its comment on verse 55 with *wa-nazala fi Qurayzah* - it came down concerning Qurayzah, a treaty people of Madinah. Al-Tabari names the same group as the model case, "like Qurayzah and their peers" among those who had a pact with the Prophet, and he records Mujahid's report that Qurayzah backed the Prophet's enemies on the day of Khandaq. Al-Muyassar identifies them as the Jews who had entered treaties with the Prophet not to fight him or aid anyone against him, then broke them time after time. So the severe language of this passage was revealed about specific, known treaty-breakers in the Prophet's own moment. The verse itself, though, describes them by behavior - those who break their pact *fi kulli marrah*, every time - and that behavioral description is what the rest of the passage builds on.
edits.evidence: al-Jalalayn 8:55: "ونَزَلَ فِي قُرَيْظَة". al-Tabari 8:56: "كقريظة ونظرائهم ممن كان بينك وبينهم عهد وعقد", and Mujahid (report 16210): "قريظة مالأوا على محمد يوم الخندق أعداءه". al-Muyassar 8:56: "مِن أولئك الأشرار اليهودُ الذين دخلوا معك في المعاهدات بأن لا يحاربوك ولا يظاهروا عليك أحدًا، ثم ينقضون عهدهم المرة تلو المرة".

edits.after:
This means the believer is not permitted to preserve righteousness by violating it. Even when betrayal is feared, the line into khiyanah is still guarded by Allah.

One more thing the classical readings make plain: who carries these commands. Al-Tabari opens verse 57 with "Allah says to His Prophet Muhammad" - the "you" of *tathqafannahum* and *fa-inbidh* is the Prophet as leader of the community. And when al-Tabari draws the general rule from verse 58, he states it at the level of leadership, not the individual: whenever signs of treachery appear from a treaty people, as they appeared from Qurayzah, "it is a duty upon the imam of the Muslims to cast [the treaty] back to them openly" - *fa-haqqun 'ala imam al-muslimin an yanbidha ilayhim 'ala sawa'* - and to give notice of war. Making treaties, ending treaties, and conduct in war sit with the community's legitimate authority. What every reader takes from these verses is the ethic - no hidden treachery, even toward the treacherous - not a personal license to act on war-and-treaty commands.

And to say it plainly: nothing in this reflection is a legal ruling, and nothing here settles any question of war, treaty, or conflict for anyone. This is a tadabbur: it reads what the passage says and reports how the commentators scoped it. For rulings, ask a qualified scholar.
edits.evidence: al-Tabari 8:58: "فكذلك حكم كل قوم أهل موادعةٍ للمؤمنين، ظهر لإمام المسلمين منهم من دلائل الغدر مثل الذي ظهرَ لرسول الله ﷺ وأصحابه من قريظة منها، فحقٌّ على إمام المسلمين أن ينبذ إليهم على سواء، ويؤذنهم بالحرب". al-Tabari 8:57: "يقول تعالى ذكره لنبيه محمد ﷺ: فإما تلقيَنَّ في الحرب هؤلاء الذين عاهدتهم فنقضوا عهدك".

edits.before: This is not a denial of their iman. The ayah explicitly calls them believers. But it distinguishes between shared faith and a fuller legal-political belonging tied to hijrah in that moment of communal formation.
edits.after:
This is not a denial of their iman. The ayah explicitly calls them believers. But it distinguishes between shared faith and a fuller legal-political belonging tied to hijrah in that moment of communal formation.

The classical commentaries add a dimension this reflection would otherwise miss: for them, this walayah included inheritance. Al-Jalalayn glosses the alliance here as being "in support and in inheritance" - *fi al-nusrah wa-al-irth* - reads "you have no walayah with them" as *fa-la irtha baynakum wa-baynahum*, no inheritance between you and them, and then adds: *wa-hadha mansukh bi-akhir al-surah* - "and this is abrogated by the end of the surah." Ibn Kathir reports the same history: the Muhajirun and Ansar, paired as brothers by the Prophet, "used to inherit from each other, having more right to inheritance than the deceased man's relatives, until Allah abrogated that practice with the fixed share for near relatives." Al-Tabari records this inheritance reading too, with reports from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and others, though his own preferred reading of the walayah in this verse is support and aid rather than estates. So on the accounts that carry it, the bond named here was real enough that for a time it redrew even inheritance - until the surah's final verse restored the claims of kin.
edits.evidence: al-Jalalayn 8:72: "﴿أُولَئِكَ بَعْضهمْ أوْلِياء بَعْض﴾ فِي النُّصْرَة والإرْث... فَلا إرْث بَيْنكُمْ وبَيْنهمْ... وهَذا مَنسُوخ بِآخِرِ السُّورَة". Ibn Kathir 8:72: "They used to inherit from each other, having more right to inheritance than the deceased man's relatives, until Allah abrogated that practice with the fixed share for near relatives." al-Tabari 8:72 records the inheritance reading with reports 16331 (Ibn 'Abbas), 16333 (Mujahid), 16335 (Qatadah), 16336 ('Ikrimah and al-Hasan), while his own gloss of the verse runs through nusrah: "بعضهم أنصار بعض، وأعوان".

This is one of the most important balancing points in the passage. Emotional solidarity does not nullify treaty obligation. Even in the face of religious sympathy, the believers may not casually violate a binding pact. Revelation refuses both coldness toward believers and chaos toward covenants.

Ibn Kathir spells the limit out: help your brothers in faith when they call for aid, "unless they ask you to aid them against disbelievers with whom you have a fixed-term treaty of peace. In that case, do not betray your treaties or break your promises" - and he notes that this explanation was reported from Ibn 'Abbas. Even shared faith does not authorize breaking a standing pact.

edits.after:
This is sobering because it strips believers of fantasy. Falsehood also forms structures. Opposition also coordinates. Hostility also builds networks of mutual protection.

The commentaries, though, scope this half-verse concretely rather than leaving it as a standing observation about the world. Ibn Kathir reads it through inheritance across the line of religion: he cites the Prophet's words that "no followers of two religions inherit from each other," recited alongside this very verse. Al-Tabari records Ibn 'Abbas saying the verse "came down concerning the inheritances of the treaty-people idolaters" - *nazalat fi mawarith mushriki ahl al-'ahd*. Al-Tabari's own preferred reading is different again: for him the verse means the disbelievers back one another as supporters, and it stands as evidence for the obligation of hijrah - a believer was not to remain settled in the land of war. And he records Qatadah tying it to the fence-sitter: the man who camped between the two camps saying, whichever side wins, I am with them - and Allah refused them that. The reading that follows below - that falsehood organizes and truth must too - is this reflection's own contemplation resting on those classical scopings, not a further classical position.
edits.evidence: Ibn Kathir 8:73: "لَا يَتَوَارَثُ أَهْلُ مِلَّتَيْنِ" / "(No followers of two religions inherit from each other...)" with the Prophet reciting this ayah. al-Tabari 8:73 report 16344 (Ibn 'Abbas): "نزلت في مواريث مشركي أهل العهد". al-Tabari's tarjih: "وأولى التأويلين... أن بعضهم أنصار بعض دون المؤمنين، وأنه دلالة على تحريم الله على المؤمن المقامَ في دار الحرب وترك الهجرة". Qatadah report 16346: "كان ينزل الرجل بين المسلمين والمشركين، فيقول: إن ظهر هؤلاء كنت معهم، وإن ظهر هؤلاء كنت معهم! فأبى الله عليهم ذلك".

edits.defect: CRITICAL: ulu al-arham inheritance/naskh reading absent + MODERATE: fi kitab Allah glossed as general charter
edits.before:
After widening the circle, the verse restores order. Spiritual belonging does not erase every other divinely assigned bond. **Al-arham** are womb-ties, blood relations, family links. The ayah protects the moral architecture of closeness from becoming vague and indiscriminate.

The phrase **fi kitabillah** grounds this precedence in divine legislation, not custom alone. Allah's Book knows how to make room for expanding brotherhood while still assigning rightful priority where He wills.
edits.after:
After widening the circle, the verse restores order. Spiritual belonging does not erase every other divinely assigned bond. **Al-arham** are womb-ties, blood relations, family links.

The commentaries read this clause as something far more specific than a general statement about family closeness: an inheritance ruling. Al-Tabari glosses it directly - those related by the womb are "more entitled to one another in inheritance," *ba'duhum awla bi-ba'din fi al-mirath*, over the sworn ally and the patron - and he records Qatadah: the believing bedouin who had not migrated could not inherit from the muhajir "until Allah sent down: and those of the wombs are more entitled to one another in the Book of Allah." Ibn Kathir names the abrogation outright: "According to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Al-Hasan, Qatadah and several others, this Ayah abrogated inheriting from those with whom one had ties of treaties or brotherhood, as was the case in the beginning of Islam." Al-Jalalayn reads the same way: more entitled "in inheritance than inheriting through the faith and hijrah mentioned in the preceding verse." On that account, the hijrah-brotherhood bonds had for a time carried estates with them, and this closing verse returned inheritance to kin.

Al-Tabari himself holds a different position on one point: he accepts that this verse assigns inheritance to womb-ties, but argues the earlier walayah verses were about support, not estates - so on his reading there is "no abrogating and no abrogated" in these closing ayahs at all. The disagreement is real, and both sides land in the same place on what this clause does: inheritance follows the womb-ties, by Allah's decree.

And **fi kitabillah** is glossed concretely by the commentaries: al-Tabari reads it as "in the ruling of Allah which He wrote in the Preserved Tablet" - *fi hukm Allah alladhi katabahu fi al-lawh al-mahfuz* - and al-Jalalayn likewise: "the Preserved Tablet... and from it is the wisdom of inheritance." The phrase points to the decreed inheritance rule itself, written before the world, not to a general charter for community bonds. The broader thought - that Allah's Book makes room for expanding brotherhood while still assigning rightful priority - can stand as this reflection's own contemplation, but the letter of the clause is about the mirath.
edits.evidence: al-Tabari 8:75: "والمتناسبون بالأرحام = ﴿بعضهم أولى ببعض﴾ ، في الميراث... من الحليف والولي = ﴿في كتاب الله﴾ ، يقول: في حكم الله الذي كتبه في اللوح المحفوظ"; Qatadah report 16353: "كان لا يرث الأعرابيُّ المهاجرَ، حتى أنزل الله: ﴿وأولوا الأرحام بعضهم أولى ببعض في كتاب الله﴾". Ibn Kathir 8:75: "According to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Al-Hasan, Qatadah and several others, this Ayah abrogated inheriting from those with whom one had ties of treaties or brotherhood." al-Jalalayn 8:75: "﴿بَعْضهمْ أوْلى بِبَعْضٍ﴾ فِي الإرْث مِن التَّوارُث فِي الإيمان والهِجْرَة المَذْكُورَة فِي الآيَة السّابِقَة ﴿فِي كِتاب اللَّه﴾ اللَّوْح المَحْفُوظ... ومِنهُ حِكْمَة المِيراث". al-Tabari's no-naskh position (on 8:74): "الدليلُ الواضح على أن لا ناسخ في هذه الآيات لشيء، ولا منسوخ".
